name: Worcester
headline: Getting to know Worcester,
street by street and hill by hill.
answer: Worcester is a city of 206,518 people (2020 Census) in Central Massachusetts and the historic seat of Worcester County. Its housing ranges from 19th-century triple-deckers to single-family homes, with 884 single-family sales in 2025. Worcester station at Union Station is the western end of the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line to Boston, and I-290 runs through the city.
overview: Worcester was incorporated as a town in 1722 and became a city in 1848, and it has served as the seat of Worcester County since 1731. That long run shows in the streets: Victorian-era mill buildings, lunch-car diners and a large stock of triple-decker houses, a building type the city is often credited with originating. Downtown gathers around Worcester Common and Union Station in Washington Square, where the Framingham/Worcester Line begins its run east to Boston's South Station.

Open space threads through the city. Elm Park, whose first 27 acres were bought in 1854, carries a plaque calling it the first purchase of land for a public park in the United States. Mass Audubon's Broad Meadow Brook covers more than 400 acres of woods, fields and marsh, and Quinsigamond State Park offers swimming beaches and a 2,000-meter rowing course on Lake Quinsigamond. The Worcester Art Museum, open since 1898, holds nearly 40,000 objects, and colleges including Clark, Holy Cross and WPI sit across the city's hills.

Worcester's planning framework is recent. The Planning Board adopted the Worcester Now | Next comprehensive plan in March 2024, and the city added broad zoning provisions for accessory dwelling units the same year. A Housing Production Plan followed: the City Council adopted it on August 19, 2025, the state approved it on March 10, 2026, and it projects a need for 12,300 more homes by 2033. In January 2025 the mayor said the city's existing zoning already met the MBTA Communities law, and the state lists Worcester as compliant. The Canal District shows the change on the ground: Polar Park opened there on May 11, 2021, and by August 2024 four apartment buildings with nearly 550 units were open or nearly finished around the ballpark.

housing.text: Worcester's Housing Production Plan, adopted by the City Council on August 19, 2025, finds that most of the city's housing was built before 1960 and that 57.9% of residents rent (ACS 2018 to 2022). The plan calls triple-deckers iconic features of the housing stock, and its data show more than 4,700 rental units added in the previous decade, mainly in traditional 3-to-4-unit buildings; the first three-deckers are credited to builder Francis Gallagher in Worcester. About 44% of the city's land is zoned exclusively for single-family homes, according to the Worcester Regional Research Bureau's summary of the plan.

villages.name: Downtown
villages.line: The city center around Lincoln Square, Federal Square, Worcester Common and Union Station in Washington Square.

villages.name: Canal District
villages.line: The northern part of the old Green Island neighborhood, between the former Blackstone Canal and Mill Brook, with the Revington apartments at Kelley Square and new buildings near Polar Park alongside historic triple-deckers and workers' cottages.

villages.name: Shrewsbury Street
villages.line: A major street running northeast from downtown to Route 9, lined with restaurants; the Boulevard Diner, a 1936 Worcester Lunch Car Company diner at 155 Shrewsbury Street, was listed on the National Register in 2000.

villages.name: Main South
villages.line: The neighborhood along Main Street south of downtown, developed from the 1850s; Jonas Gilman Clark founded Clark University here in 1887.

villages.name: Grafton Hill
villages.line: Also called Union Hill (originally Sagatabscot Hill), one of the city's seven hills, in southeastern Worcester along Grafton and Providence Streets.

villages.name: Greendale
villages.line: A North Worcester neighborhood along West Boylston Street, where the Greendale Village Improvement Society's hall at 480 West Boylston Street was listed on the National Register in 1976.

villages.name: Quinsigamond Village
villages.line: A former mill village in the Blackstone River valley along Millbury Street, grown around Washburn & Moen's South Works (1846 to 1977), with three-deckers, Victorian double cottages from 1875 to 1878 and a 1913 branch library.

commute.text: Worcester station is the western end of the Framingham/Worcester Line, with stops through Grafton, Westborough and Framingham to Boston's South Station. I-290 runs through the city and meets the Massachusetts Turnpike (I-90) and I-395 just south in Auburn.

places.name: Elm Park
places.line: About 58 acres with Newton Hill, ponds, trails, a disc golf course and summer concerts; its original 27 acres were bought in 1854.

places.name: Worcester Art Museum
places.line: Open since 1898 at 55 Salisbury Street, with a collection of nearly 40,000 objects.

places.name: Broad Meadow Brook Wildlife Sanctuary
places.line: Mass Audubon's large urban sanctuary at 414 Massasoit Road, with trails through woods, fields, streams and marsh.

places.name: Quinsigamond State Park
places.line: Two DCR sites on Lake Quinsigamond, Regatta Point and Lake Park, with swimming, sailing, picnicking and a 2,000-meter rowing course.

places.name: Green Hill Park
places.line: The city's largest park, listed by the city at 470 acres, with an 18-hole municipal golf course opened in 1929, a free year-round farm, the 30-acre Green Hill Pond and the Massachusetts Vietnam Veterans' Memorial, dedicated in 2002.

places.name: Union Station
places.line: A French Renaissance Revival station by Watson & Huckel at 2 Washington Square, opened in 1911, restored for $32 million and reopened to MBTA and Amtrak trains in 2000.

places.name: Polar Park
places.line: The Worcester Red Sox ballpark at 100 Madison Street in the Canal District, opened on May 11, 2021, as part of the redevelopment of Kelley Square and the Canal District.

places.name: EcoTarium
places.line: A science and nature museum on 60 acres, founded in 1825 as the Worcester Lyceum of Natural History, with a planetarium, outdoor wildlife exhibits and a narrow-gauge train.

history.text: Incorporated as a town on June 14.
Isaiah Thomas gave the first public reading of the Declaration of Independence in Massachusetts on July 14.
The Blackstone Canal opened, and the city's industry grew along it.
The railroad to Boston opened, the start of the city's role as a rail hub.
Incorporated as a city on February 29.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Worcester, MA?
faq.a: The median single-family sale price in Worcester for calendar year 2025 was $430,000, across 884 sales, up from $420,000 in 2024, according to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town report.
Yes. Worcester station at Union Station, 2 Washington Square, is the western end of the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line, which runs to Boston's South Station.
Worcester Public Schools. Review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Worcester, MA?
faq.a: For fiscal year 2026, Worcester's tax rate is $13.28 per $1,000 of assessed value for residential property and $29.06 per $1,000 for commercial, industrial and personal property, according to the city's Taxes & Assessments page.

faq.q: What kinds of homes are in Worcester?
faq.a: Most of Worcester's housing was built before 1960, and triple-deckers are a defining type; the city's 2025 Housing Production Plan reports more than 4,700 rental units added in the previous decade, mainly in 3-to-4-unit buildings. Single-family homes also trade in volume: The Warren Group counted 884 single-family sales in 2025.
